10.1002_adma.74091: Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) are capable of electrochemically converting fossil fuels such as natural gas and coal‐based syngas directly into electricity with high efficiency and minimal emissions, yet the state‐of‐the‐art nickel‐based anodes are susceptible to sulfur poisoning or coking when operated with sulfur‐containing or hydrocarbon fuels. Here, we report a high‐entropy strategy in which five equimolar cations are introduced at the A‐site to develop a highly active and robust perovskite anode, Pr 0.2 Ba 0.2 La 0.2 Sr 0.2 Ca 0.2 FeO 3‐δ (PBLSCF). In situ reduction of PBLSCF leads to the exsolution of nanoscale Fe particles, enhancing its tolerance to sulfur poisoning and coking. Electrolyte‐supported single cells using PBLSCF anodes achieve a peak power density (PPD) of 1.22 W cm −2 at 800°C in H 2 , maintain stable operation for 1000 h and exhibit promising sulfur tolerance in 50 ppm H 2 S‐H 2 . Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the high‐entropy strategy reduces oxygen‐vacancy formation energy, contributing to improved sulfur tolerance and fuel oxidation performance. Furthermore, stable operation using a PBLSCF anode for 600 h is also achieved with propane as fuel. This work provides a synergistic strategy through A‐site high‐entropy engineering and in situ metal exsolution to achieve promising electrochemical performance and enhanced multi‐tolerance anodes for fuel‐flexible SOFCs.
10.1002_anie.8724105: The design of a low‐Ir‐loading anode catalyst with high activity and stability is crucial for the proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE), yet it remains a formidable challenge. Herein, an ordered Ba 2 EuIrO 6 double perovskite is demonstrated as a promising anode material for catalyzing oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in acid electrolyte. The Ba 2 EuIrO 6 achieves a low overpotential of 250 mV at 10 mA cm −2 and high mass activity with 1.39 A mg −1 toward OER, outperforming BaIrO 3 and commercial IrO 2 catalysts. It is discovered that the oxygen bridged Ir─O bri ─Eu unit in Ba 2 EuIrO 6 plays a critical role as the catalytically active center. In situ spectroscopic studies, isotope labeling measurements and theoretical calculations reveal that the Ir─O bri ─Eu units possess strong proton affinity for proton capture from OOH* and OH*, triggering the bridging oxygen‐mediated deprotonation mechanism to break traditional scaling relationships during the OER. Furthermore, the incorporation of Eu modulates the Ir d z2 orbital to increase the spin density of adsorbed oxygen, accelerating ─OH attack and reducing the energy barrier for OOH* formation. The Ba 2 EuIrO 6 ‐loading PEMWE delivers over 1.0 A cm −2 at only 1.67 V and operates stably for 350 h at 1.0 A cm −2 , demonstrating its good potential for practical applications.
10.1016_j.ijhydene.2026.157369: Alkaline water electrolysis is central to decarbonising hard-to-abate sectors, and its economics benefit from exploiting both dispatch flexibility and waste-heat recovery. Mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) is widely used for electrolyser dispatch optimisation, yet many formulations assume constant efficiency and neglect temperature-dependent part-load behaviour. This paper presents an MILP-compatible framework, derived from a semi-empirical electrochemical model, that captures the dependence of performance on current density and temperature. Three surrogates of increasing fidelity, a temperature-constant piecewise-linear (PWL) model, a tangent-plane (TAN) approximation, and a novel triangulated convex-combination (TRI) approach preserving the full current density-temperature surface, are compared in a generic case study maximising operational profit from hydrogen sales, electricity export, and heat utilisation under dynamic thermal constraints. Annual hydrogen production and operational profit are moderately affected by surrogate choice, whereas recoverable waste heat differs by up to 30% across formulations: simpler surrogates misrepresent thermal behaviour under part-load and dynamic conditions. PWL remains adequate for hydrogen-oriented dispatch, TAN offers a pragmatic compromise where temperature is required as a state variable, and TRI provides the most informative basis where waste-heat recovery and part-load consistency are the focus.
10.1016_j.jechem.2026.07.071: The instability of aqueous Zn metal anodes originates from the coupled failure of interfacial chemistry and deposition crystallography, where water-rich Helmholtz planes trigger parasitic reactions while disordered Zn nucleation accelerates dendrite growth. Conventional electrolyte additives mainly regulate solvation or interfacial adsorption, but rarely integrate Helmholtz plane reconstruction with crystallographic texture control. Herein, we propose a bioinspired zincophilic electrolyte engineering strategy using L-theanine (TN), a naturally derived biomolecule, to construct a dynamically stabilized anode-electrolyte interface. Spectroscopic analyses, in-situ diagnostics, molecular dynamics simulations, and density functional theory calculations demonstrate that TN coordinates with Zn 2+ , disrupts the Zn 2+ -H 2 O interaction, and reconstructs the outer Helmholtz plane by partially replacing coordinated water. Simultaneously, TN preferentially adsorbs at the inner Helmholtz plane and forms a water/sulfate-repellent interfacial layer, which suppresses hydrogen evolution, electrode corrosion, and zinc hydroxysulfate formation. Beyond chemical passivation, the TN-derived adaptive layer homogenizes interfacial ion flux and promotes Zn adatom self-diffusion, inducing dendrite-free Zn deposition with a favorable (002)-oriented texture. Consequently, Zn|TN-0.2|Zn cells operate stably for over 4000 h, and Zn|TN-0.2|Cu cells achieve an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.5% for 1400 cycles. Moreover, Zn|TN-0.2|I 2 @C full cells retain 95.2% capacity after 20,000 cycles at 10 A g −1 . This work advances electrolyte additive design from single-factor interfacial protection toward bioinspired molecular programming of both Helmholtz chemistry and Zn deposition texture.
10.1016_j.joule.2026.102531: Silicon-graphite (Si/Gr) anodes increase battery energy density, but rapid Si "burn-out" limits lifetime. Yet, battery management systems lack effective tools to diagnose Si aging beyond capacity loss and to manage its degradation during operation. Here, we develop a diagnostic framework that jointly estimates material-specific health and degradation-induced Si open-circuit potential deformation from constant-current charge data. The framework tracks the transition state-of-charge (SoC) below which Si dominates, revealing pathway-dependent Si utilization shifts: from 48% fresh to 73% with lithium loss but 33% with active-Si loss. Transition SoC error remains below 3% up to an effective 0.3C, and error bounds across sampling and charge windows support onboard use. Guided by the finding that elevated temperature improves Si capacity retention in our cells, we propose adaptive thermal management that warms the cell during Si-dominant operation and cools it otherwise, projecting an approximately doubled cycle life without limiting capacity access.
10.1016_j.seppur.2026.140717: Mixed matrix membranes are a promising strategy to overcome the permeability–selectivity trade-off in polymer-based gas separation membranes. In this work, nitrogen-doped biochars derived from chitosan are incorporated at low loadings (1, 2, and 5 wt%) into carboxylated polymers of intrinsic microporosity to fabricate Mixed matrix membranes with enhanced gas separation performance. Gas sorption–diffusion measurements for CO₂, H₂, CH₄, and N₂ reveal a pronounced, gas-dependent effect of carbon incorporation: relative to the neat caPIM membrane, at 5 wt% filler CO₂ solubility increases, CH₄ solubility decreases, and H₂ solubility remains comparable or slightly lower. In parallel, the diffusivities of CO₂, CH₄, and especially H₂ increase, whereas N₂ diffusivity is markedly reduced, leading to higher CO₂ and H₂ permeabilities combined with strong N₂ rejection over the investigated pressure range. The combined effects of selective sorption and polymer–filler diffusion result in outstanding separation performance. The membrane containing 5 wt% nitrogen-doped biochar achieves high ideal selectivities, up to ~ 67 for CO₂/N₂ and in the 10 2 –10 3 range for H₂/N₂, surpassing Robeson's upper bound for the H₂/N₂ gas pair. These results demonstrate that the biochar acts as a functional, sorption-active phase whose accessible microporosity and surface chemistry cooperatively interact with the caPIM matrix. Overall, nitrogen-doped, bio-derived carbons emerge as intrinsically compatible and selective fillers for high-performance MMMs, offering a sustainable platform for post-combustion CO₂ capture and hydrogen purification from nitrogen-rich gas streams.
10.1021_jacs.5c17338: Fullerene (C 60 ) exhibits rich redox chemistry but suffers from severe dissolution of reduced fulleride species in carbonate electrolytes, leading to poor reversibility and rapid capacity fading. Here, we demonstrate covalent bridging as a general strategy to stabilize the fullerene framework using Mg 4 C 60 . Mg atoms promote intercage covalent connections through C–C single bonds and [2 + 2] cycloaddition bonds, transforming a van der Waals molecular solid into a layered polymeric framework. Comprehensive characterizations reveal that such bridging effectively suppresses dissolution, preserves structural integrity, and enables a reversible Li + storage process. Interestingly, unlike pristine C 60 that undergoes multiple phase transitions, Mg 4 C 60 exhibits slope-type electrochemical profiles reminiscent of soft carbon yet originates from an ordered two-dimensional framework. Comprehensive mechanistic studies reveal reversible fullerene cage distortions accompanied by the dynamic reconstruction of sp 2 electronic states, while the covalently bridged scaffold remains intact. This work establishes covalently bridged fullerenes as a new class of durable carbonaceous anodes and provides a general pathway for designing ordered carbon frameworks with enhanced stability for next-generation rechargeable batteries.
